510.s: Relatives played organ, piano and violin; his parents came from St. Martin and the house was full of Calypso.
510.ch: Early life and path to music
510.q: Yeah, matter of fact my uncle played organ and keyboard, he was a swinging organ player. He lived in Washington and he used to play some jobs over there. My mom played a little piano. My grandmother played a little violin. Nothing serious. And they actually did make an attempt to send me and my…

1013.t: Show business childhood and a musical family
1013.s: Childhood acquaintances in show business, seeing uncles on TV, mother's stride piano, an uncle arranging at 14, a cousin drumming with Toto.
1013.q: Where do you go from there? And my childhood acquaintances were Nat King Cole and Judy Garland and the Andrews Sisters and Sophie Tucker, Jack Benny. So without knowing who they were, I was being imbued with this culture of music, you know, show business, music. And it just seemed like a natural…

655.t: Italian musical family and deciding on drums at four
655.s: Swing, jazz, Italian folk and opera at home, musical grandparents and cousins, and a vision at four that he would play drums.
655.q: Well that from my parents, and also the indigenous Italian folk music and some opera and my sister, who is about six years older than I am, she listened to the pop music of the day. So I had a fairly good cross section of music.

888.t: Growing up in a musical family
888.s: Her parents and relatives played piano; she learned 'Sweet Sue' at nine or ten and got formal lessons two years later.
888.q: Yes. Um hum. I grew up in a home where there was music all of the time. My dad played piano, my mom played, and my aunts and uncles played, and there was a song called “Sweet Sue” that my dad used to play all of the time. And I learned to play that song. I guess I must have been about nine or ten…

495.t: Starting guitar at seven; Italian family and music
495.s: Bertoncini began at seven on his father's guitar; his Italian parents from Emilia Romagna, Parma and Verdi, and family music at Christmas.
495.q: Yeah, my dad had a guitar around the house. He was from Italy and he used to sing Italian folk songs. And it was always around and I just took to it. Well I just considered that a great gift you know. I don’t quite understand that either.

987.t: Father's jam sessions, Clifford Brown and Bobby Mojica
987.s: Asked for an AHA moment, Brecker describes his pianist father's jam sessions, record collection, neighbors, Bobby Mojica and Clifford Brown in Philly, and his wariness of music as a life.
987.q: Well that’s a good question. Like I said, my father was a semi-professional pianist, very good songwriter/singer, knew a lot of musicians in Philly and there were jam sessions at the house. And the level was really pretty damn high. He had a great record collection. By luck our next door neighbor…

437.t: Father the keyboardist who tried to keep him out of music
437.s: Born 1950, he grew up with jazz records; his legally blind father tried to steer him away from music, but he took up drums.
437.ch: Growing up with his father and Joe Morello
437.q: Before I was born my father was a professional musician. And he was friends with Phil Woods, the famous jazz saxophone player, Sal Salvador, a great jazz guitarist, and Joe Morello, a phenomenal drummer. And he used to always be playing their records or the records of the jazz masters all the time.…

538.t: Born into a musical Boston family
538.s: Carrington says she never saw another path; her grandfather and father played drums and saxophone, her father nurtured her timekeeping, and she grew up on blues-based jazz.
538.q: Well this may have something to do with it, as far as decided early, we have a lot to do in the way of fate but we can I think help direct it but there is also sometimes some universal power that directs it for you. 131.t: Italian and Irish heritage; swing records and jukeboxes
131.s: His ancestry, grandfather's violin, and the swing-era music of his early years; the move to Buffalo in 1949.
131.q: Well I mean first of all I was 4 years old when it started so I don’t know if it was swing or big band. I can’t really recall the word “jazz” until later on. 321.t: The piano in the house and his father's button accordion
321.s: His brother moved a piano into the house, showed him middle C, and his father played Slovak button accordion polkas.
321.q: Yeah. My brother was finishing his college degree when I was about 5 or 6 years old, or he was in college and he moved a piano into our house, and there was a piano because he needed it for whatever you need to do to pass piano in college. So there it was. And Joe showed me middle C and some notes,…

890.t: Starting music in wartime New Orleans and the Gabriel family line
890.s: Gabriel says he began playing in 1943 when younger players were away at war, and describes four generations of musicians: Santo Domingo-born great-grandfather, uncles Percy and Clarence, drummer father, saxophonist mother.
890.ch: Growing up in a musical family
890.q: Oh I played behind them early, later in life I was playing behind them after I left New Orleans and went to Detroit. But I started playing music in New Orleans in 1943 during the war. The war was going on and all the musicians that were able to go to the war, were 20 or 25, they were all gone so…

326.t: Family, move to California and how the trombone came into the family
326.s: One of five children taught piano by his mother; the family drives to Hollywood, brother Al gets a trombone from Earle Hagen, and it passes to Jack and then Urbie at 12.
326.q: Well I was one of five children and we had a mother that played the piano a little bit, and so she started each one of us with the basics of playing the piano. My brother Al was about, let’s see, I started when I was about five I guess. We all started about that same age. And my brother Al, who was…

332.t: Growing up in wartime London: the battered piano and disapproving parents
332.s: Ingham describes the bomb-damaged family piano, starting to play at eight, and parents who saw jazz as youth rebellion, like a 78 titled 'DJC Blues'.
332.ch: Opening and early jazz in England

530.t: Crowley family, Professor O'Jay and Illinois Jacquet
530.s: Jordan's family was not very musical; his teacher Professor O'Jay taught Illinois Jacquet, and Jacquet's honking and screaming opened Jordan to playing free and high notes.
530.q: No they wasn’t. They, in fact my father now, I didn’t come from New Orleans, I came from a little town they called Crowley, Louisiana. And he had some cousins that played. But my daddy used to get, on a Saturday night sometimes when he had a few little drinks in him, he would pick up accordion and…

608.t: Natural love of music and the one-hour practice limit
608.s: Early memories of music, Soloff and Rubin calling him a natural, and neighbors' complaints limiting practice to an hour.
608.q: Not get better, but two things that I’m going to mention at this clinic I’m doing for mostly rock & rollers, a couple of jazzers, this Friday, a couple of days from now, in Northampton, that I had mentioned to you. 721.t: Childhood record player, toy soldiers and the 1812 Overture
721.s: Malone recalls playing war with his brother in Hawaii to 1812 Overture and getting his own violin at five.
721.q: Yes, yes. I was living in Hawaii at the time, I was four or five years old and I heard all this music and yeah, we used to play war. My dad was a military officer. We used to play war. My brother and I used to play war and my brother got a violin and, you know, because of listening to that music,…

1003.t: Musical family and first trumpet lessons on Long Island
1003.s: Music filled the house; an uncle studied with Doc Cheatham, Nick got a trumpet, studied with Felix Sangenito and played Italian weddings and political events as a kid.
1003.q: Great question, and I did think about that. I’ll be honest with you I thought about that before this interview. I’ve been truly, truly blessed to come from a family, not so much of musicians although there were some, two of the paternal great, great, great whatever back in Italy were bandmasters.…

1015.t: Jazz guitarist father and music-teacher mother
1015.s: His father was a jazz guitarist who wept over Charlie Christian solos, and his mother a music teacher; Moore grew up on jazz records.
1015.q: Yeah, it was. My father was a jazz guitarist and a very good one. And my mother was a vocal music teacher and piano major and taught piano and taught music, actually was my music teacher in elementary school when I was going to school. So yeah, I grew up listening to a lot of great jazz records,…

1047.t: Teaching artist work and a family of teachers
1047.s: She loves teaching; her mother and grandmother were educators.
1047.q: I love it. Well I’ve been told that teaching is in my blood. My mother is a teacher, my grandmother was a teacher, an educator, a professor, but also a nurse. And she was a head nurse to teach other nurses. And education is just really important. It was important to me. It changed my life. And I…

443.t: Playing second trumpet in his father's polka band, and polka links to jazz
443.s: He sat with his father's Austro-Hungarian polka band at picnics, and sees polka as close to two-beat jazz, as in Germany, and in Ken Peplowski's background.
443.q: Yeah. I think it just became a natural thing and he played in a polka band, he had come over from Austria-Hungry, so I’m really first generation American. And every Sunday during the summer months he would be playing with a polka band at picnics and stuff, and I would sit alongside him and play…

889.t: Family music: father's Italian feast band
889.s: His father, uncles all musicians; he began on drums at eight in his father's Italian feast band and ended up on trumpet.
889.q: Okay well yeah, in my household my father is a musician. He was a saxophone player. His brother, my uncle, was a drummer. And my other uncle was an arranger and a piano player and he played tuba. And my father had the Italian feast bands where they, you know, they always pin the money on the thing.…

660.t: Father's wedding-party band and starting on trumpet
660.s: Ries was a curious child in Michigan; his father worked in a factory and gigged on weekends, taking him along. Ries wanted to play trumpet like him.
660.q: I was. I grew up in Michigan and my father played the trumpet and my mother played piano. I had three sisters, they all took piano lessons. 992.s: Her grandmother taught piano; the family was musical but jazz was absent; childhood fascination with Christmas lights.
992.q: Well my grandmother was a piano teacher so I think all — my brother, my cousins, we all went through her teaching. The only one who stuck with it was me. So that’s how it worked. But I have it, in a certain way, family, like a musical family. My dad plays some piano because his mother played piano.…

410.s: Early piano lessons, then seeing Teddy Wilson at a Hackensack restaurant; his parents befriend Wilson, Hank Jones and Eddie Durham and trust them as mentors.
410.q: Right. And John Thompson, “A Day in Bermuda” or whatever they called it. “A snowy Bird” you know, and learned all that stuff. And then, on this Benny Goodman record I listened to it and I looked at all the names and then in my local newspaper, the Bergen Evening Record I saw, I was about, I don’t…

812.t: Her father Sammy and singing in Woonsocket
812.s: Prompted by a tune, she describes her trombonist father Sammy, his weekend band, her early singing and the songs he wrote out for her.
812.q: [sings] “perhaps someone else may be nearer/your heart.” Interesting that you should do that one. It’s not one — it’s not necessarily a staple that I have played throughout, and I’m not even sure I can recall that many people asking for it, but it was a song that I sang a lot in my home in…

361.t: Uncle Joe, the family jazz pianist in Rochester
361.s: Frank describes his uncle Joe playing swing piano at Sunday family dinners and the tunes he played.
361.q: Yes. There was a piano player that — well first, before anything, my uncle on my father’s side, one of his younger brothers, his name was Joe, and he was a jazz pianist, and a very good one, a very good one. So I was brought up listening to him as a little kid, like five or six years old. I used to…

108.t: Father's sousaphone and the musical family
108.s: Earliest memories of music: his father's cornet, tuba and sousaphone, bands rehearsing at the house, and brother Curtis on bass.
108.ch: Childhood and learning music in Philadelphia
108.q: My earliest memories are my father. My father played – he originally played cornet. I don’t recall – I don’t remember him – that might have been before I was born. He played sousaphone. He studied the tuba and played that. That I do remember, because he always had this sousaphone around his neck,…

387.t: Nyack childhood and the neighbors' bells
387.s: Not a musical family; the boy is fascinated by a neighboring family's set of bells near Nyack.
387.q: Early on though I do remember there was a family, a very famous painter who had a farm up on Congers, Andrew Davies, and the kids used to walk to Nyack from their farm. They still have a very good farm.
